answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the closing line of “On Clothes,” a chapter of Kahlil Gibran’s The Prophet (1923), confirmed against the Project Gutenberg text of the book.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Some of you say, ‘It is the north wind who has woven the clothes we wear.’ And I say, Ay, it was the north wind, But shame was his loom, and the softening of the sinews was his thread. And when his work was done he laughed in the forest. Forget not that modesty is for a shield against the eye of the unclean. And when the unclean shall be no more, what were modesty but a fetter and a fouling of the mind? And forget not that the earth delights to feel your bare feet and the winds long to play with your hair.
trail: First published in 1923 by Alfred A. Knopf as part of The Prophet, confirmed in the Project Gutenberg catalog entry ↗.
The exact sentence appears verbatim in the “On Clothes” chapter as reproduced by the Project Gutenberg text ↗.
Independently corroborated by the Academy of American Poets ↗, which credits the line to The Prophet (Knopf, 1923).
A third transcription at monadnock.net ↗ matches the same wording, ruling out a single corrupted source.
source.excerptNote: The popular quote form usually drops the opening “And” and is presented as a standalone sentence; in the original it closes a longer passage on modesty and clothing.
source.rightsNote: The Prophet was first published in 1923, more than 95 years before 2026, so it has entered the public domain in the United States; no separate translation is involved since Gibran wrote the book directly in English.

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: About Kahlil Gibran
author.bio: Kahlil Gibran was born in Ottoman-ruled Mount Lebanon and emigrated to Boston as a child. He is best known for The Prophet (1923), a book of twenty-six prose-poem discourses that became one of the best-selling books of the twentieth century and remains one of the most translated works in history.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This line is not disputed as to authorship — it is a genuine sentence from Gibran’s own book. The only common distortion is cosmetic: the popular quote-card version almost always drops the leading conjunction and punctuation that ties it to the preceding sentence in the original.

items.who: Popular quote sites and social media
items.why: Typically render the line as a free-standing aphorism, “Forget not that the earth delights to feel your bare feet and the winds long to play with your hair,” omitting the opening “And” that connects it to Gibran’s preceding sentences on modesty in the original chapter ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is authentically Gibran’s, from “On Clothes” in The Prophet (1923); only its usual stripped-down, standalone presentation differs from the original text, as shown in the full chapter ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: “On Clothes” is one of the twenty-six short discourses that make up The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran’s 1923 book in which the fictional prophet Almustafa answers the people of Orphalese on subjects from love to death before departing by ship. Asked to “speak to us of Clothes,” Almustafa argues that garments are as much a shield of shame and habit as they are protection, and closes the passage by urging his listeners not to let clothing sever them from direct, physical contact with the natural world.

This exact sentence closes that discourse, immediately following Gibran’s lines on modesty as “a shield against the eye of the unclean.” It is one of the most widely circulated single lines from The Prophet on social media and inspirational-quote sites, almost always presented on its own and stripped of the leading “And” that opens it in the original text.
